assessments.statement: Within two days the UK's line on the US-announced energy ceasefire moved from welcoming it and relaying Ukraine's readiness to implement it, to treating Russia's continued strikes as proof it has no interest in peace and answering with pressure on partners and faster missile deliveries.

The air-defence acceleration announced is small next to existing commitments: £10 million of a £45 million package brought forward, within £1.6 billion already committed over four years, with the larger sanctions, military and fiscal packages still being drawn up.

Burnham's Scotland offer carries his English devolution model north, explicitly including local control of transport, procurement, innovation funding and employment support, and casts Holyrood, not only Westminster, as part of the centralisation problem.

The offer's first real test is the National Economic Council meeting with the devolved First Ministers due a couple of weeks after 16 October; so far the one concrete Scottish Government agreement the speech reported is matching £10 million for two defence technical colleges.

statements.text: On 12 October the Prime Minister told the Commons he welcomed President Trump's announcement of a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and said President Zelenskyy had assured him Ukraine would implement it as soon as a start date was confirmed.

By the Downing Street meeting on 14 October the tone had hardened: the two leaders spoke of Russia's indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure since Trump's call, and said Russia had no interest in peace. The UK had already moved to urging partners to press Putin to respect the US call.

The practical response was faster deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles against jet-powered drones. But the sums are modest: £10 million of a £45 million package brought forward, within £1.6 billion already committed over four years. The larger sanctions, military and fiscal packages are still being drawn up.

At home, the clearest thread is how much of Burnham's Greater Manchester record, where he was Mayor until June, he is offering Scotland. He cited his buses under public control built in Falkirk, English mayors' control of innovation funding, and localised employment support, now offered to Scotland's regions.

The pitch casts Holyrood, not only Westminster, as part of the problem. He called Scotland one of the most centralised nations in Europe and asked both governments to push power out from the centre, which makes the offer awkward for the Scottish Government to accept.

He called it a serious and genuine offer. Its first test is the National Economic Council meeting with the devolved First Ministers, due a couple of weeks after 16 October and the first since he took office. So far the one concrete agreement the speech reported is Edinburgh matching £10 million for two defence technical colleges.

The next fixed date after that is the UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November. The Prime Minister used it in his Scotland pitch as well, as the food and farming deal, and told the Commons he wants a serious dialogue about long-term options for the relationship to follow it.
